body:
Meaning of interoperability

Interoperability is the ability of different organisations, systems and personnel to exchange and use information and work together effectively.

Disaster response often involves several departments and institutions. An alert may originate with a scientific agency, be received by disaster management authorities, and require action by district administration, police, fire services, health facilities and local communities.

These organisations do not necessarily use the same equipment, maps, contact lists or reporting systems. Interoperability helps them develop a shared understanding of the situation and coordinate their actions.

What effective coordination requires

  • Clear responsibilities: Participants know which institution provides information, makes decisions and carries out assigned actions.
  • Compatible information: Reports use understandable locations, timestamps and agreed descriptions.
  • Reliable communication: Agencies can exchange urgent information and use backup arrangements when ordinary channels fail.
  • Shared situational awareness: Different teams work from verified information about hazards, affected areas and available resources.
  • Tested coordination: Exercises reveal whether information and instructions reach the correct organisations.

For example, a district flood map may show that access to a hospital is threatened. The district administration, health department, transport authorities and hospital management need to use consistent information while deciding what arrangements are appropriate.

Institutional responsibilities in India and Gujarat

InstitutionCore role relevant to this topic
National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA)National disaster management policies, plans, guidelines and preparedness initiatives
State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA)State-level disaster management planning and coordination
District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA)District-level planning, preparedness and coordination
Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority (GSDMA)Gujarat's state disaster management planning, preparedness and coordination
Gujarat Institute of Disaster Management (GIDM)Disaster management training, research and capacity building
National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC)Satellite-based observations, mapping and geospatial decision support
National Disaster Response Force (NDRF)Specialised disaster response and associated training and exercises

The Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) supports communication, information management and coordination during emergencies. Its importance lies in helping responsible institutions maintain a common understanding and carry out their respective duties.

GSDMA and GIDM should not be confused. GSDMA is the state disaster management authority, while GIDM is an institution focused on training and capacity development.

Gujarat examples of multi-agency preparedness

Gujarat's disaster management arrangements reflect the state's exposure to hazards such as cyclones, floods, earthquakes and industrial accidents. Districts with industrial installations may need particular attention to coordination between industrial management and the surrounding public authorities.

GSDMA's published disaster management programme information records a chemical-disaster mock exercise on 21 November 2025 covering Bharuch, Surat, Kachchh, Morbi, Jamnagar and Devbhumi Dwarka. The example illustrates how industrial-disaster preparedness may require participation across multiple districts.

Another documented example is the 25 February 2026 multi-agency mock exercise at Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel International Airport, Ahmedabad. The exercise simulated an earthquake and associated consequences to evaluate coordination, communication and response arrangements among participating agencies.

These are dated examples of preparedness activities, not evidence that an identical exercise is conducted on a fixed schedule everywhere.

After-action review and continuous improvement

An exercise or actual emergency provides information about how a plan worked. This information becomes valuable when it produces specific changes.

An after-action review examines what was intended, what occurred, what worked and what needs improvement. Findings may be recorded in an after-action report.

Common weaknesses may include outdated contact details, conflicting instructions, inaccessible assembly locations, delays in sharing information or inadequate consideration of people requiring assistance.

Turning findings into improvements

  1. Record: Describe an observed problem using evidence from the exercise.
  2. Explain: Identify the reason for the problem rather than merely noting that performance was unsatisfactory.
  3. Assign: Identify who is responsible for correcting the problem and when the correction should be completed.
  4. Update: Revise the relevant plan, contact list, training material or working arrangement.
  5. Retest: Check in a later exercise whether the correction is effective.

For example, if an exercise finds that a hospital did not receive a simulated district warning, repeating the same exercise without improving the communication arrangement achieves little. Updating the contact system, checking alternative channels and testing them again creates a meaningful improvement.

Connecting technology with capacity building

Technology and preparedness strengthen each other. Remote sensing and field reports improve the available information. GIS and decision-support systems help people interpret it. Telecommunications deliver warnings. Training and exercises enable institutions and communities to act. After-action learning improves the next round of monitoring, decisions and preparedness.

The practical test of a disaster management system is not whether it possesses advanced technology, but whether reliable information reaches responsible people and leads to suitable protective action.

Prelims focus

  • Interoperability means that different institutions or systems can exchange information and work together.
  • NDMA, SDMAs and DDMAs operate at national, state and district levels respectively.
  • GSDMA handles state disaster management functions; GIDM focuses on training and capacity building.
  • Emergency Operations Centres support information sharing and coordination.
  • After-action reviews identify gaps that should lead to assigned and tested improvements.
  • Trap: A completed mock drill does not prove that the disaster management plan is effective unless its performance is evaluated and weaknesses are addressed.

[Sources: NDMA, Guidelines on Disaster Management Exercises, as explained in the Press Information Bureau note dated 10 August 2025, inter-agency coordination and post-exercise follow-up sections; GSDMA, Chapter XVII, Disaster Risk Management Programme and Mock Drills sections; Press Information Bureau, SVPIA Conducts Multi-Agency Mock Exercise to Strengthen Disaster Preparedness, 25 February 2026; GIDM, Training and Capacity Building section; NRSC, Disaster Management Support, Overview; Gujarat and national institutional information consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Hazard information flows through analysis and alerts to prepared institutions and protective action, while after-action learning strengthens capacity.
pictures.caption: Disaster risk reduction depends on a continuous connection between information, institutions, action and learning.

title: Interoperability, Gujarat Institutions and Learning After Disaster Exercises
